t: Metadata Reconstruction Tool: a plain-language overview
title: Metadata Reconstruction Tool: a plain-language overview
description: Overview: what the Metadata Reconstruction Tool does and why archives need it. A metadata reconstruction tool rebuilds the information that should have traveled with a file but got lost: when it was made, who made it, what it is about. It hunts for clues in the filename, inside the file itself, and in neighboring records like manifests and catalogs. The scattered clues become one complete metadata record.
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.

t: How the Metadata Reconstruction Tool works
title: How the Metadata Reconstruction Tool works
description: Overview: what the Metadata Reconstruction Tool does and why archives need it. Real reconstruction combines several evidence streams: filename parsing with regular expressions pulls dates, sequence numbers, and project codes from names like '2024-03-15_field-trip_042.jpg'; embedded properties (EXIF, XMP, ID3, PDF info dictionaries) supply camera settings, authors, and timestamps; and manifest or catalog joins link files to their descriptive records. Each candidate fact gets a confidence score and a source note, and conflicts are resolved by source priority — embedded data usually outranks filename guesses. The merged result follows a schema like Dublin Core.
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.

t: How the Metadata Reconstruction Tool works: the deep tour
title: How the Metadata Reconstruction Tool works: the deep tour
description: Overview: what the Metadata Reconstruction Tool does and why archives need it. Real reconstruction combines several evidence streams: filename parsing with regular expressions pulls dates, sequence numbers, and project codes from names like '2024-03-15_field-trip_042.jpg'; embedded properties (EXIF, XMP, ID3, PDF info dictionaries) supply camera settings, authors, and timestamps; and manifest or catalog joins link files to their descriptive records. Each candidate fact gets a confidence score and a source note, and conflicts are resolved by source priority — embedded data usually outranks filename guesses. The merged result follows a schema like Dublin Core. Advanced tools learn filename grammars per collection instead of hand-writing patterns, detect timestamp tampering by cross-checking EXIF against filesystem dates, and propagate metadata across related files (every page scan in a folder inherits the folder's event description). Quality is measured by field-level accuracy against archivist-verified records. The limits are genuinely destroyed metadata — overwritten EXIF, renamed files with no pattern — which the tool must report as unknown rather than invent, because a fabricated date is worse than a missing one.
